name: Ahithophel
title: David's counselor who became a traitor
summary: Ahithophel from Giloh in Judah was one of the most influential advisors at King David's court, and his insight was so highly valued that it was regarded as equal to a divine oracle (2 Sam 16:23). He was the father of Eliam, who was likely identical with Bathsheba's father—making Ahithophel Bathsheba's grandfather. When Absalom rose in rebellion against David, Ahithophel defected to Absalom's side, possibly driven by personal bitterness over David's abuse of Bathsheba and the killing of Uriah. Ahithophel advised Absalom with both political and military sharpness: he recommended publicly taking possession of David's concubines to mark an irreversible break, and then proposed an immediate attack on the fleeing David. It was Hushai—David's secret ally—who managed to persuade Absalom to reject this advice, which the biblical text attributes to the Lord's guidance. When Ahithophel realized that his strategic plan had been discarded and the rebellion's downfall sealed, he returned home to Giloh, set his house in order, and took his own life by hanging. In Christian interpretive history, his fate has often been seen as a typological precursor to Judas Iscariot's betrayal of Jesus.

keyEvents.title: David's highly respected counselor
keyEvents.description: Ahithophel served as one of King David's most trusted advisors. His counsel was regarded as being as valuable as a word from God himself.

keyEvents.title: Joins Absalom's rebellion
keyEvents.description: When Absalom rebelled against his father David, Ahithophel chose to support Absalom. This was a heavy blow to David, who prayed that Ahithophel's counsel might be turned into foolishness.

keyEvents.title: Ahithophel Advises Absalom to Take David's Concubines
keyEvents.description: Ahithophel advised Absalom to go in publicly to David's concubines to show that the break with his father was irreversible, thereby strengthening Absalom's position.

keyEvents.title: His Counsel to Pursue David
keyEvents.description: Ahithophel proposed pursuing David immediately with 12,000 men to kill him while he was weak and exhausted. This was a militarily wise counsel that could have decided the rebellion.

keyEvents.title: Hushai Counters Ahithophel's Counsel
keyEvents.description: Hushai, who was loyal to David and served as his secret agent, persuaded Absalom to reject Ahithophel's counsel and follow another strategy. The Lord directed this to frustrate Absalom's plans.

keyEvents.title: Ahithophel's Suicide
keyEvents.description: When Ahithophel saw that his counsel was not followed, he understood that Absalom's rebellion would fail. He went home to Giloh, set his affairs in order, and hanged himself. He was buried in his father's tomb.

versions.summary: Ahithophel was a highly respected advisor to King David from the town of Giloh. He was known for his exceptional wisdom, and his counsel was regarded as an oracle from God. However, he betrayed David and joined Absalom's rebellion, taking his own life when his advice was rejected.
versions.title: David's counselor who became a traitor
versions.reason: [minor] The role 'servant' is very general and not very descriptive of Ahithophel's position. He was primarily a political advisor, not an ordinary servant. 'Royal counselor' would have been more precise. In addition, the role 'traitor' is missing, which is a central part of his story.; [minor] Eliam is correctly mentioned as Ahithophel's son (2 Sam 23:34). It may be worth noting the possible connection to Bathsheba, who according to 2 Sam 11:3 was the daughter of Eliam – which would in that case make Ahithophel Bathsheba's grandfather. This is an important possible family relationship.; [major] The profile completely lacks footnotes. There are several interesting historical, linguistic, and theological aspects regarding Ahithophel that should be covered, including his possible kinship with Bathsheba, parallels to Judas Iscariot, and the significance of his name.; [minor] The life period 'ca. 1040-970 BC' is reasonable, but given that Absalom's rebellion likely took place around 975-970 BC, and Ahithophel died during this rebellion, the year of death could be adjusted somewhat. The period is still acceptable as an approximation.; [minor] It could have been useful to include Psalm 41:10 and Psalm 55:13-15 as possible references where David laments over his treacherous friend, which is traditionally understood as a reference to Ahithophel.

versions.summary: Ahithophel was a highly respected advisor to King David from the town of Giloh in Judah. He was known for his exceptional wisdom, and his counsel was regarded as an oracle from God himself (2 Sam 16:23). He was the father of Eliam, and possibly the grandfather of Bathsheba. When Absalom rebelled against David, Ahithophel joined the rebellion—possibly motivated by bitterness over David's treatment of Bathsheba and Uriah. His military advice to pursue David immediately was strategically wise, but it was opposed by Hushai, who was David's secret agent. When Ahithophel realized that his counsel had been rejected and that the rebellion was therefore doomed to fail, he returned home to Giloh, settled his affairs, and hanged himself. His fate is often seen as a typological parallel to Judas Iscariot.

versions.reason: [minor] The lifespan 'c. 1040–970 BC' is somewhat uncertain. Absalom's rebellion is usually dated to c. 976–970 BC, and Ahithophel died during this revolt. A birth date around 1040 BC would make him about 65–70 years old, which is reasonable but difficult to determine precisely. The use of 'c.' is appropriate, though the death year could be adjusted slightly, for example to 'c. 1040–975 BC', to better align with common datings of Absalom's rebellion.; [minor] The summary is very similar to the previous version (starting identically with "Ahithophel was a highly respected advisor to King David from the town of Giloh"). Since there is an earlier version with a score of 6, the text should be rephrased more clearly to distinguish it from that one.; [minor] The role "traitor" is correct from the narrative's perspective, but one might consider adding "military strategist," given that his military counsel is a central element in the story.; [minor] The archaeological footnote about Giloh refers to Joshua 15:51 and provides geographical information. However, it is primarily a geographical/historical identification rather than an archaeological discovery. The source type "historical" could have been more precise, but "archaeological" is acceptable since it concerns the location of the place.

versions.reason: [minor] The lifespan of 'ca. 1040–975 BC' is reasonable but somewhat uncertain. Given that Absalom's rebellion is typically dated to ca. 975–970 BC, and Ahithophel took his own life during the rebellion, the death date is acceptable. The birth date is purely speculative but within reasonable limits.; [minor] The word 'guddommeleg' is a Nynorsk form, while the rest of the text is consistently in Bokmål. It should be written as 'guddommelig' for consistency.; [minor] The role 'military strategist' is debatable – Ahithophel gave military-strategic advice during the rebellion, but his primary role was that of an advisor, not a military strategist in the traditional sense. Nevertheless, it is defensible to retain this role given his concrete military counsel in 2 Sam 17:1-4.; [minor] The footnotes are very thorough and good. However, the archaeological footnote about Gilo is more geo-historical than archaeological, since no specific archaeological findings are referenced. The category 'historical' would have been more precise.

footnotes.text: The Hebrew expression in 2 Sam 16:23 – 'as if one were asking a word from God' (כַּאֲשֶׁר יִשְׁאַל אִישׁ בִּדְבַר הָאֱלֹהִים) – uses the verb שׁאל (sha'al), which is also the technical term for oracle inquiries in the Old Testament. This places Ahithophel's counsel on a level with priestly oracle delivery, a remarkable feature in a secular advisor context.

Ahithophel's act of 'setting his house in order' (2 Sam 17:23) before taking his life suggests a deliberate and planned action rather than an impulsive reaction. The Hebrew expression (וַיְצַו אֶל־בֵּיתוֹ) implies that he gave instructions regarding his household and property, which was an act typically associated with someone preparing for death.

In rabbinic tradition (Sanhedrin 101b-102a), Ahithophel is discussed as an example of a wise man who used his wisdom for evil. Some rabbinic sources suggest that his wisdom was so great that he could have been counted among the wise in Israel, but that his pride and desire for revenge led to his downfall.
